newsitem.title: USA: Challenges seen in U.S.-China relations - Lord.
newsitem.headline: Challenges seen in U.S.-China relations - Lord.

text.p: A leading State Department official on Tuesday called China "the most difficult regime we have had to deal with" in 25 years and said Chinese suspicions of the United States contributed to testy relations.

U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for East Asian and Pacific Affairs Winston Lord, in a speech here, said China will pose a monumental challenge to any U.S. administration in the coming years because of its new assertiveness.
He told the Japan Society that China has no experience of dealing with outside world as an equal and is using nationalism to fill the ideological void left by discredited Marxism.

"It is the most difficult regime we have to deal with throughout the 25-year period," he said. Lord was one of the first U.S. officials to visit China in the 1970s with then-Secretary of State Henry Kissinger and later served as ambassador to Beijing.
China's suspicion that the United States is out to contain China and to keep it from becoming a super power contributes to a "difficult mood," Lord noted.
But it is to China's best interest to keep a peaceful relationship with the U.S., he said.

With one-third of its exports destined for the United States and a $35 billion trade surplus, China needs Washington economically. The United States also provides a geopolitical counterbalance as China remains concerned about resurgence of nationalism in Russia and Japan's remilitarization, Lord said.
"The relationship will be sweet and sour," he said.

Calm has prevailed since China mounted live-missiles excercise in the Taiwan Strait in the run-up to Taiwan's presidential election earlier this year and the U.S. responded by sending aircraft carriers to patrol the sea lane.
But Lord said the immediate relationship between China and Taiwan, which Beijing regards as a renegade province, "does not look too great."
Besides Taiwa, human rights in China and situation in Hong Kong after its reversion to Chinese sovereignty in 1997 could also complicate U.S.-China relations, he said.
Lord noted that there is a bipartisan consensus on the need for dialogue with China.
"A summit meeting in 1997 or beyond is possible, so are vice presidential trips," he said.
Lord will accompany Secretary of State Warren Christopher to China next month.
